newsitem.title: USA: Former astronaut John Glenn to quit U.S. Senate.
newsitem.headline: Former astronaut John Glenn to quit U.S. Senate.

text.p: Sen. John Glenn, the first American to orbit the Earth, announced his retirement on Thursday, opening the way for a battle for his seat that could spell bad news for his fellow Democrats.

The 75-year-old former astronaut returned to his hometown 35 years to the day after his historic space flight and told a hall filled with young people that advancing age, and only that, was forcing him to step down.

"For all the advances, there's one immutable problem that we will never solve -- there's no cure for the common birthday," the four-term senator said. A fifth term "would take me to the age of 83. For that reason and for that reason alone I have chosen not to seek another term."

Glenn became the first American to orbit Earth on Feb. 20, 1962, ten months after Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin did so. Glenn made three orbits in five hours before his Mercury spacecraft landed in the Atlantic Ocean near the Bahamas.

George Voinovich, Ohio's popular two-term Republican governor and the man regarded as having the surest shot of capturing Glenn's seat for his party, issued a statement saying Glenn was a "true American hero."

Voinovich, who has made plans to seek the Senate nomination but is not yet a formal candidate, made no mention of his political plans in the statement. Under Ohio law the former Cleveland mayor cannot serve a third consecutive term.
"John Glenn's place in our nation's history is secure," he added.
Sen. Mike DeWine, an Ohio Republican, said Glenn had "put his service to America before anything else. (He is) truly a modern American pioneer."
At the moment the Democrats lack anyone with the state-wide organisation and appeal that Voinovich has to put up as Glenn's successor. The Republicans currently hold a 55-45 edge in the Senate.
Glenn urged the 700 students filling Brown Chapel at Miskingum College not to fall victim to a cynicism that, he said, was eating at the United States.

"I feel saddened when I hear people say America is headed in the wrong direction and there is no hope of righting it," he said. "I am most concerned about the signal this sends to young people like yourselves...

"In a thousand dffferent ways and on a countless different battlefields you can fight battles every bit as important as those my generation fought and build a future that is truly worthy of our past," he said.
Glenn was first elected to the Senate in 1974. He unsuccessfully sought his party's presidential nomination in 1984.
